summary: Defines MIB objects for managing character stream devices, such as serial terminal ports, using SMIv2. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Gauges for checking the plain text ports on a machine.

questions: what is a character stream device
subtitle: SNMP objects for managing terminal-style ports and the sessions that run over them.

tldr.problem: Systems such as terminal servers have ports that carry streams of characters, and network managers had no standard way to inspect or control them remotely.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the Character MIB in SMIv2: one base object and two tables, one row per port and one row per session, covering state, flow control, character counts and session control.
tldr.outcome: The MIB is mandatory for all systems that offer character stream ports. It obsoletes RFC 1316.

today: RFC 1658 is a Draft Standard and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 1316.

sections.title: Introduction and Framework
sections.content:
RFC 1658 defines an extension to the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing character stream devices. It is written for the SNMPv2 Network Management Framework, which the memo lists as four parts: RFC 1442 (the SMI, which describes and names managed objects), STD 17 RFC 1213 (MIB-II, the core set of objects), RFC 1445 (administrative and architectural aspects) and RFC 1448 (the protocol used to reach managed objects).

Objects are defined with the subset of ASN.1 that the SMI permits. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and the object type together with an instance identifies one specific instantiation of the object. The module itself, called char, sits at { mib-2 19 }.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a big catalog of things on a network that a manager can look at. This memo adds a new page to the catalog, for text ports.

sections.title: Ports and Sessions
sections.content:
The Character MIB applies to any port that carries a character stream, whether physical or virtual, serial or parallel, synchronous or asynchronous. The most common example is a hardware terminal port with an RS-232 interface. Another is a parallel printer port, for instance with a Centronics interface. Virtual terminal ports, such as a software connection point for a remote console, also count.

The MIB is mandatory for all systems that offer character stream ports, for example terminal servers, general-purpose time-sharing hosts, and even a bridge with a virtual console port.

Its central abstraction is the port. Physical ports match hardware ports one to one; virtual ports are software entities with no hardware connector. Each port supports one or more sessions, a virtual connection that carries characters between the port and some partner, typically over a stack of network protocols. A typical session is Telnet over TCP.

The MIB has one base object and two tables, for ports and for sessions. It deliberately makes no distinction between permanent and operational data; how to treat that is implementation specific.
sections.plainLanguage: A port is a socket on the machine where a keyboard and screen can plug in. A session is one conversation going through that socket. A socket can have one or more conversations at a time.

sections.title: The Port Table
sections.content:
The base object charNumber counts the entries in charPortTable, regardless of their state. Each row, indexed by charPortIndex, describes one port. The index is a PortIndex: a unique value greater than zero, recommended to be assigned contiguously from 1. Where the port sits on hardware that has an ifIndex, it is conventional but not required to make the two equal.

Key per-port objects include:

  • charPortName, an administratively assigned name of up to 32 characters, and charPortType, either physical or virtual.
  • charPortHardware, a pointer to a hardware-specific MIB subtree such as one for RS-232; it returns the null identifier { 0 0 } if none is configured.
  • charPortReset, a control that clears the port and disconnects its sessions when set to execute. Reads always return ready.
  • charPortAdminStatus (enabled, disabled, off, maintenance) as the desired state, and charPortOperStatus (up, down, maintenance, absent, active) as the actual state. These map onto ifAdminStatus and ifOperStatus values.
  • charPortInCharacters and charPortOutCharacters, 32-bit counters of characters seen, including framing, flow control characters and each BREAK.
  • charPortAdminOrigin (dynamic, network, local, none), which says where sessions may start, and charPortSessionMaximum, where -1 means no maximum.
  • charPortLowerIfIndex, the ifIndex of the hardware beneath the port, or zero if none.

Flow control is reported with charPortInFlowState and charPortOutFlowState (none, unknown, stop, go). The older single-valued charPortInFlowType and charPortOutFlowType are marked deprecated in favor of charPortInFlowTypes and charPortOutFlowTypes. These one-octet values are sums: 128 for xonXoff, 64 for enqHost and 32 for enqTerm, with zero meaning no flow control.
sections.plainLanguage: Each port gets a report card: its name, whether it is switched on, whether it is really working, how many letters went in and out, and whether it has been told to stop talking for a moment.

sections.title: The Session Table
sections.content:
Each row of charSessTable describes one session and is indexed by the pair charSessPortIndex and charSessIndex. Every port has charPortSessionNumber, a gauge of open sessions that are connecting, connected or disconnecting, and charPortSessionIndex, which gives the first or only active session (zero if there is none).

  • charSessState is connecting, connected or disconnecting, ignoring flow control.
  • charSessKill works like the port reset: reads return ready, and setting execute terminates the session.
  • charSessProtocol names the network protocol in use. The memo assigns identifiers under wellKnownProtocols for other, Telnet, Rlogin, LAT, X29 and VTP.
  • charSessOperOrigin records whether the session was started from the network, locally, or from an unknown source.
  • charSessInCharacters and charSessOutCharacters are each session's share of the port counters.
  • charSessConnectionId points to related MIB information, for example tcpConnState for a TCP connection when no Telnet MIB exists; it returns { 0 0 } if unavailable.
  • charSessStartTime is the sysUpTime value when the session entered the connecting state.
sections.plainLanguage: Each conversation gets its own card too: is it starting, running or ending, what language it is speaking, who started it, and a button that ends it.

sections.title: Relation to the Interface MIB
sections.content:
The Character MIB does not relate directly to the Interface MIB, because a character port is not intrinsically a network interface. In most implementations it sits above a physical sublayer interface, such as the RS-232-like or parallel-printer-like MIBs, which are represented by a row in ifTable identified by ifIndex. The objects charPortLowerIfIndex and the status mappings mentioned above are the links between the two. The memo lists RFC 1659 (RS-232-like devices) and RFC 1660 (parallel-printer-like devices) among its references.

Conformance is stated through charCompliance, which makes one object group, charGroup, mandatory for SNMPv2 entities with character hardware interfaces. The group lists the current port and session objects and leaves out the two deprecated flow type objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The text port usually plugs into a lower-level wire connection that has its own MIB page. This memo says how to point from one page to the other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo's security section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. Note that the MIB does include writable objects, such as the port reset and session kill controls, but the text says nothing about protecting them.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not say how to stop the wrong person from pressing the reset buttons.
